facts.statement: Henry Fairfield Osborn formally described Oviraptor in 1924.
facts.quote: These were formally described by the North American paleontologist Henry Fairfield Osborn in 1924

facts.statement: The type species Oviraptor philoceratops was established based on the holotype specimen AMNH 6517.
facts.quote: The particular genus Oviraptor was erected with the type species O. philoceratops based on the holotype AMNH 6517

facts.statement: Henry Osborn named the genus Oviraptor, meaning "egg seizer" or "egg thief" in Latin, based on his initial interpretation that the dinosaur was eating eggs.
facts.quote: Osborn interpreted Oviraptor as a dinosaur with egg-eating habits, and explained that the generic name, Oviraptor, is Latin for "egg seizer" or "egg thief", due to the association of the fossils

facts.statement: The specific name philoceratops means "fondness for ceratopsian eggs," reflecting the original belief that the nest belonged to a Protoceratops or similar dinosaur.
facts.quote: The specific name, philoceratops, is intended as "fondness for ceratopsian eggs" which is also given as a result of the initial thought of the nest pertaining to Protoceratops or another ceratopsian

facts.statement: In 1976, Rinchen Barsbold concluded that Oviraptor was distinct from ornithomimids based on anatomical traits.
facts.quote: In 1976, the Mongolian paleontologist Rinchen Barsbold noted some inconsistencies regarding the taxonomic placement of Oviraptor and concluded that this taxon was quite distinct from ornithomimids based on anatomical traits

facts.statement: In 1986, Rinchen Barsbold determined that two specimens previously referred to Oviraptor actually belonged to a new genus, Conchoraptor.
facts.quote: In 1986, Barsbold realized that the latter two did not belong to the genus and instead they represented a new oviraptorid: Conchoraptor

facts.statement: In 2010, Nicholas R. Longrich and colleagues expressed uncertainty about referring a Chinese specimen to Oviraptor due to anatomical differences in hand proportions.
facts.quote: In 2010 Nicholas R. Longrich and the two latter paleontologist have expressed their uncertainties regarding this referral as there are several anatomical differences such as the hand phalangeal proportions

facts.statement: In 1981, Rinchen Barsbold referred the well-preserved specimen MPC-D 100/42 to Oviraptor.
facts.quote: In 1981, Barsbold referred the specimen MPC-D 100/42 to Oviraptor, a very well-preserved and rather complete individual from the Djadokhta Formation

facts.statement: Rinchen Barsbold described a second species, Oviraptor mongoliensis, in 1986 based on specimen MPC-D 100/32a from the Nemegt Formation.
facts.quote: In 1986, Barsbold described a second species of Oviraptor, "O. mongoliensis", based on specimen MPC-D 100/32a which hails from the Nemegt Formation

facts.statement: In 1997, Rinchen Barsbold re-examined the specimen O. mongoliensis and found it distinct enough to name a new genus, Rinchenia, though it remained a nomen dubium.
facts.quote: However, a re-examination by Barsbold in 1997 found enough differences in this specimen to name the new genus Rinchenia, but he did not describe it with formality and this new oviraptorid remained as a nomen dubium

facts.statement: In 2004, Halszka Osmólska and colleagues formally named the taxon Rinchenia mongoliensis.
facts.quote: This was amended by the Polish paleontologist Halszka Osmólska and team in 2004 by formally naming the taxon Rinchenia mongoliensis

facts.statement: In 2018, Mark A. Norell and colleagues reported a new Oviraptor specimen, AMNH 33092, consisting of a tibia and two metatarsals from a nestling or small juvenile.
facts.quote: The North American paleontologist Mark A. Norell and colleagues in 2018 reported a new specimen of Oviraptor: AMNH 33092, which is composed of a tibia and two metatarsals of a nestling or very small juvenile

facts.statement: Henry Osborn originally assigned Oviraptor to the family Ornithomimidae, though this was later found to be incorrect.
facts.quote: The initial relationships of Oviraptor were poorly understood at the time and was assigned to the unrelated Ornithomimidae by the original describer, Henry Osborn

facts.statement: Oviraptor likely had two well-developed hindlimbs ending in three functional toes with a vestigial first toe and a relatively reduced tail.
facts.quote: Though the holotype largely lacks the posterior region of the skeleton, it is likely that Oviraptor had two well-developed hindlimbs that ended in three functional toes with the first one being vestigial, as well as a relatively reduced tail

facts.statement: Related oviraptorids show that Oviraptor's arms were covered in elongated feathers and its tail ended in a pygostyle supporting a fan of feathers.
facts.quote: As evidenced in related oviraptorids, the arms were covered by elongated feathers, and the tail ended in a pygostyle, which is known to support a fan of feathers

facts.statement: It is debated whether a Chinese specimen from the Bayan Mandahu Formation belongs to Oviraptor, as researchers noted anatomical differences in hand proportions.
facts.quote: However, in 2010 Nicholas R. Longrich and the two latter paleontologist have expressed their uncertainties regarding this referral as there are several anatomical differences such as the hand phalangeal proportions

facts.statement: The skull of Oviraptor is deep, shortened, and has large openings, measuring approximately 17.9 centimeters in length as preserved.
facts.quote: The skull of Oviraptor was deep and shortened with large fenestrae (openings) compared to other dinosaurs, and measures about 17.9 cm (7.03125 in) long as preserved.

facts.statement: Although the holotype skull lacks a crest, bone surface evidence suggests Oviraptor likely had a well-developed crest supported by nasal and premaxilla bones.
facts.quote: The holotype skull lacks a crest in almost its entirety, however, the top surfaces of the fused parietal and frontal bones indicate that it likely had a well-developed crest, supported by the nasal and premaxilla bones (mainly the latter) of the rostrum.

facts.statement: Oviraptor possessed toothless jaws ending in a robust, parrot-like horny beak called a rhamphotheca.
facts.quote: Oviraptor had toothless jaws that ended in a robust, parrot-like rhamphotheca (horny beak).

facts.statement: The lower jaw of Oviraptor is a short and deep bone covering approximately 19.5 centimeters.
facts.quote: As a whole, the lower jaw is a short and deep bone that covers 19.5 cm.

facts.statement: The scapula of Oviraptor is slightly bowed and measures 23 centimeters in length.
facts.quote: The scapula is slightly bowed and measures 23 cm in length.

facts.statement: Oviraptor's hand had three skinny, bird-like fingers, each ending in a side-to-side flattened and recurved claw.
facts.quote: The hand of Oviraptor had three skinny and bird-like fingers with each finger ended in side to side flattened and recurved unguals (claw bone).

facts.statement: A nest associated with Oviraptor preserves elongatoolithid eggs that are approximately 14 centimeters long.
facts.quote: The nest AMNH 6508 preserves elongatoolithid eggs, with each egg being 14 cm long (some are incomplete).

facts.statement: Henry Fairfield Osborn originally classified Oviraptor with ornithomimids because of its toothless beak.
facts.quote: Oviraptor was originally allied with the ornithomimids by Osborn due to its toothless beak.

facts.statement: In 1976, Rinchen Barsbold established the family Oviraptoridae, designating Oviraptor as its type genus.
facts.quote: In 1976, Barsbold erected a new family to contain Oviraptor and its close kin, making Oviraptor the type genus of the Oviraptoridae.

facts.statement: In 1977, Rinchen Barsbold proposed that Oviraptor's robust jaws and beak were strong enough to crush mollusk shells like clams found in its geological formation.
facts.quote: In 1977, Barsbold proposed a crushing jaw hypothesis. He argued that the strength of the robust lower jaws and likely rhamphotheca (horny beak) was strong enough to break the shells of mollusks such as clams, which are found in the same geological formation as Oviraptor.

facts.statement: David K. Smith rejected the crushing jaw hypothesis in 1990, arguing that Oviraptor's jaws preserved shearing surfaces rather than a crushing mechanism.
facts.quote: In a 1990 conference abstract, David K. Smith presented an osteological reevaluation of Oviraptor where he rejected the statements made by Barsbold. He found no evidence indicating a forelimb specialized in aquatic locomotion, and the jaws, rather than preserve a crushing mechanism, preserve shearing surfaces.

facts.statement: In 1995, researchers reported lizard remains in the body cavity of a holotype Oviraptor, suggesting it was partially carnivorous.
facts.quote: However, in 1995, Norell and colleagues reported the fragmented remains of a lizard in the body cavity of the holotype specimen, suggesting that Oviraptor was partially carnivorous.

facts.statement: Stig Olav K. Jansen suggested Oviraptor was omnivorous, capable of catching and tearing small prey with its beak and forelimbs.
facts.quote: Jansen suggested that oviraptorids were omnivorous as the sharply developed rhamphotheca together with the prominent forelimbs would have been adapted to catch and tear small prey.

facts.statement: In 2010, Longrich and colleagues rejected the shell-crushing hypothesis for Oviraptor, noting that durophagous animals typically have broad crushing teeth.
facts.quote: Longrich and colleagues in 2010 also rejected a durophagous (animals that practise shell-crushing) hypothesis, given that such animals typically develop teeth with broad crushing surfaces.

facts.statement: Oviraptorids share cranial features with dicynodonts, including short, deep, toothless mandibles and pointed palates.
facts.quote: The team also found that oviraptorids and dicynodonts share cranial features such as short, deep, and toothless mandibles; elongated dentary symphyses; elongated mandibular openings; and a pointed palate.

facts.statement: Funston and colleagues suggested Oviraptor had a frugivorous diet incorporating nuts and seeds based on its anatomical traits.
facts.quote: Funston and colleagues considered these anatomical traits of oviraptorids to be consistent with a frugivorous diet that incorporated nuts and seeds.

facts.statement: Research published in 1994 revealed that oviraptorids like Oviraptor brooded their nests rather than stealing eggs.
facts.quote: Since the description of the embryonic Citipati specimen in 1994, oviraptorids became more understood: instead of having been egg-eating animals, they actually brooded and cared for the nests.

facts.statement: The holotype of Oviraptor is believed to be a sexually mature individual that died while incubating a nest of eggs.
facts.quote: This specimen showed that the holotype of Oviraptor was likely a sexually mature individual that perished incubating the associated nest with eggs.

facts.statement: A new nesting oviraptorid specimen was described by Dong and Currie in 1996 from the Bayan Mandahu Formation.
facts.quote: In 1996, Dong and Currie described a new nesting oviraptorid specimen from the Bayan Mandahu Formation.

facts.statement: Researchers suggested that the nesting oviraptorid specimen was caught and buried by a sandstorm while incubating its eggs.
facts.quote: Dong and Currie suggested that it was caught and buried by a sandstorm during incubation.

facts.statement: Scientists ruled out the egg-thief hypothesis for oviraptorids because such animals would have consumed or abandoned the nest before a sandstorm could bury it.
facts.quote: They ruled out the possibility of oviraptorids being egg-thieves as they would have either consumed or instinctively abandoned the nest long before it was buried by a sandstorm or another meteorological phenomenon.

facts.statement: In 1999, Clark and colleagues provided a detailed description of the Citipati nesting specimen and discussed its association with the Oviraptor holotype nest AMNH 6508.
facts.quote: In 1999 Clark and team described in detail the previously reported Citipati nesting specimen and briefly discussed the holotype specimen of Oviraptor and its association with the nest AMNH 6508.

facts.statement: Analysis of the nest structure indicates that eggs were laid in pairs within at least three rings, forming an originally circular mound.
facts.quote: Moreover, the semicircular arrangement of the nest indicates that the eggs were laid in pairs and in at least three rings, and this nest was originally circular, similar to a mound.

facts.statement: In 2004, Hopp and Orsen analyzed oviraptorid brooding behavior to investigate why wing and tail feathers elongated in these species.
facts.quote: Thomas P. Hopp and Mark J. Orsen in 2004 analyzed the brooding behavior of extinct and extant dinosaur species, including oviraptorids, in order to evaluate the reason for the elongation and development of wing and tail feathers.

facts.statement: Based on nesting posture, Hopp and Orsen suggested that long pennaceous feathers and a full feather covering were likely present in living oviraptorids.
facts.quote: Hopp and Orsen indicated that long pennaceous feathers and a feather covering were most likely present in life.

facts.statement: Hopp and Orsen proposed that the wings and tails of oviraptorids provided protection for eggs and hatchlings against sunlight, wind, and rain.
facts.quote: The "wings" and tail of oviraptorids would have granted protection for the eggs and hatchlings against climate factors like the sunlight, wind, and rainfalls.

facts.statement: Hopp and Orsen proposed that brooding was the ancestral reason for the elongation of wings and tails in oviraptorids to protect eggs and juveniles.
facts.quote: Based on the forelimb position of nesting oviraptorids, Hopp and Orsen proposed brooding as the ancestral reason behind wing and tail feather elongation, as there was a greater need to provide optimal protection for eggs and juveniles.

facts.statement: Evidence suggests that oviraptorids had two functional oviducts but ovulated only one egg per oviduct.
facts.quote: The size and position of the eggs suggest that oviraptorids retained two functional oviducts, but had reduced the number of eggs ovulated to one per oviduct.

facts.statement: In 2008, Varricchio and colleagues noted that the large clutch sizes of oviraptorids resemble those of modern polygamous birds with extensive male parental care.
facts.quote: David J. Varricchio and colleagues in 2008 found that the relatively large egg clutch-size of oviraptorids and troodontids is most similar to those of modern birds that practice polygamous mating and extensive male parental care, such as ratite birds, suggesting similar habits.

facts.statement: Several oviraptorosaurs and oviraptorids ended their tails in pygostyles, a bony structure used in modern birds to support a feather fan.
facts.quote: The tail of several oviraptorosaurs and oviraptorids ended in pygostyles, a bony structure at the end of the tail that, at least in modern birds, is used to support a feather fan.

facts.statement: In 2018, Yang and colleagues identified cuticle layers on the eggshells of maniraptoran dinosaurs, including oviraptorids.
facts.quote: In 2018, Tzu-Ruei Yang and colleagues identified cuticle layers on several egg-shells of maniraptoran dinosaurs including those of oviraptorids.

facts.statement: Yang and colleagues suggested that cuticle-coated eggs were a reproductive strategy adapted for enhancing hatching success in the arid environments where oviraptorids lived.
facts.quote: As most oviraptorid specimens have been found in formations of caliche-based sedimentation, Yang and colleagues suggested that the cuticle-coated eggs would have been a reproductive strategy adapted for enhancing their hatching success in such arid climates and environments.

facts.statement: Yang and colleagues noted that adult specimens found with nests might be laying eggs rather than incubating them, and the multi-ring clutch design prevented sufficient heat transfer to inner eggs.
facts.quote: They noted that adult oviraptorid specimens in association with nest were not necessarily incubating the eggs as they could represent a female in the process of laying eggs, and the multi-ring clutch prevented sufficient heat transfer from the parent to the inner rings of eggs.

facts.statement: An average oviraptorid nest was a gently inclined mound with eggs arranged in pairs within three to four elliptical rings.
facts.quote: An average oviraptorid nest was built as a gently inclined mound with a highly organized architecture: the eggs were likely pigmented and arranged in pairs with each pair arranged in three to four elliptical rings.

facts.statement: Yang and colleagues concluded that the unique oviraptorid nesting style lacks modern analogs and may not be the best example for understanding bird reproductive evolution.
facts.quote: Yang and colleagues concluded the oviraptorid nesting style was so unique that they lack modern analogs, therefore, using oviraptorid reproduction may not be the best example to inform about the evolution of bird reproductive strategies.

facts.statement: Oviraptor is known from the Bayn Dzak locality of the Djadokhta Formation in Mongolia, dating to the Late Cretaceous between 71 and 75 million years ago.
facts.quote: Oviraptor is known from the Bayn Dzak locality of the Djadokhta Formation in Mongolia, a formation that dates back to the Late Cretaceous about 71 million to 75 million years ago.

facts.statement: The semiarid steppe landscape of the Djadokhta Formation was drained by intermittent streams, affected by dust and sandstorms, and had seasonal moisture.
facts.quote: The semiarid steppe landscape was drained by intermittent streams and was sometimes affected by dust and sandstorms, and moisture was seasonal.

facts.statement: It is thought that later in the Campanian and into the Maastrichtian, the climate shifted to a more humid fluvial environment similar to the Nemegt Formation.
facts.quote: Furthermore, it is thought that later in the Campanian age and into the Maastrichtian, the climate would shift to the more humid fluvial environment seen in the Nemegt Formation.

facts.statement: Oviraptor remains come from the Bayn Dzak member, which also yielded dinosaurs such as Bainoceratops, Pinacosaurus, Protoceratops, Saurornithoides, Velociraptor, and Halszkaraptor.
facts.quote: The known remains of Oviraptor have been produced by the Bayn Dzak member, which has also yielded the dinosaurs Bainoceratops, Pinacosaurus, Protoceratops, Saurornithoides, Velociraptor, and Halszkaraptor.

facts.statement: The holotype's pose and egg association suggest it was trapped over a nest during a sandstorm, leading to rapid burial before scavenging or disarticulation.
facts.quote: The pose of the holotype of Oviraptor along with the association of eggs, suggest that it was trapped over the nest during a sandstorm, and burial was relatively rapid given that the body had no opportunity to become fully disarticulated or scavenged by predators.

facts.statement: Paleontologist Kenneth Carpenter agreed that sandstorms were the most likely event to bury the eggs found in the deposits.
facts.quote: The paleontologist Kenneth Carpenter also agreed in that sandstorms may have been the most likely event that the eggs found in the deposits were buried.

facts.statement: The skull of the Oviraptor holotype became particularly flattened and distorted during fossilization.
facts.quote: Among elements, the skull have become particularly flattened and distorted during the fossilization process.
